approaches.name: Pediatric anterior approach to the distal humerus
approaches.region: anterior pediatric elbow and distal arm
approaches.corridor: Anterior lazy-Z exposure along the appropriate border of biceps: medial for brachial artery and median nerve, lateral for radial nerve

sources.title: The Pulseless Supracondylar Elbow Fracture: A Rational Approach
Management of the pediatric pulseless supracondylar humeral fracture

procedure_applications.condition: A persistently dysvascular limb or defined nerve-entrapment concern requires direct exploration after reduction and stabilization

positioning.text: Position supine with the arm on a radiolucent support and the antecubital region accessible to orthopedic and vascular teams.

setup.text: Document a structured preoperative motor, sensory, pulse, Doppler, temperature, color, and capillary-refill examination and confirm vascular expertise and repair capability.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the antecubital crease, biceps tendon, medial and lateral biceps borders, brachial pulse, and traumatic wound or skin-pucker site.

incision.text: Use a limited lazy-Z anterior incision for closed injury; incorporate and safely extend an existing open wound when present.

superficial_interval.text: Develop the interval beside biceps according to the target structure while protecting superficial veins and cutaneous nerves.

deep_interval.text: Work medial to biceps for brachial artery or median nerve and along the lateral biceps-brachioradialis border for radial nerve; do not divide the pediatric biceps tendon.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous antecubital tissue, biceps-border interval, disrupted brachialis/fascia, then fracture and neurovascular bundle.

structures_encountered.text: Biceps, brachialis, brachial artery, median nerve, radial nerve, brachioradialis, and displaced distal-humeral fragments may be encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Brachial artery, median/anterior interosseous nerve, radial nerve, superficial veins, and the biceps tendon are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Stabilize the fracture before definitive vessel or nerve repair and reassess perfusion after reduction; a persistently pale, cool, poorly perfused hand requires urgent exploration.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract biceps rather than dividing its tendon and avoid traction or clamp injury to an entrapped or contused neurovascular structure.

exposure.text: Provides direct access to brachial artery and median nerve medially or radial nerve laterally after severe supracondylar displacement.

limitations.text: This is a targeted neurovascular exploration rather than the routine exposure for supracondylar fracture fixation.

extensions.text: Extend the lateral interval distally toward radial-nerve division or extend the medial interval only enough for safe vascular control and repair.

indications.text: Indications include persistent dysvascularity after reduction/fixation and selected open injuries or new post-reduction nerve deficits with suspected entrapment.

relative_contraindications.text: A well-perfused pulseless hand or isolated initial neurapraxia is not by itself an automatic indication for exploration; management requires serial examination and individualized judgment.

implant_implications.text: Reassess the hand after provisional reduction and each wire; remove and redirect any wire temporally associated with new ischemia or nerve dysfunction.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Maintain imaging access for reduction and stable pin fixation before definitive vascular or nerve repair.

closure.text: Confirm flow and nerve continuity without compression, then close loosely with fine absorbable pediatric sutures and continue documented serial neurovascular checks.

complications.text: Complications include persistent ischemia, thrombosis, compartment syndrome, Volkmann contracture, median/radial neuropathy, stiffness, infection, and iatrogenic vessel injury.

bailouts.text: If primary arterial repair is not possible, obtain proximal/distal control and proceed with vascular reconstruction rather than accepting inadequate perfusion.

questions.question: Which biceps border exposes the brachial artery?
Which finding most clearly mandates exploration?
questions.answer: Persistent poor perfusion with a pale, cool, pulseless hand after reduction and fixation.

questions.question: Should the pediatric biceps tendon be divided?

approaches.name: Pediatric lateral approach to the distal humerus
approaches.corridor: Between brachioradialis and triceps proximally, continuing anterior to anconeus along the posterior border of the extensor mass

sources.title: Current Concepts in the Treatment of Lateral Condyle Fractures in Children
Open reduction of pediatric lateral condyle fractures: a systematic review

procedure_applications.condition: A displaced or incongruent lateral-condyle fracture requires open articular reduction
A displaced capitellar fracture requires direct lateral access

positioning.text: Position supine with arm on radiolucent support, elbow freely mobile, and imaging available for AP, lateral, oblique, and arthrogram assessment.

setup.text: Plan fixation and arthrogram use while prioritizing preservation of the posterolateral soft-tissue attachments that supply the fragment.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark lateral supracondylar ridge, lateral epicondyle, capitellum, radial head, proximal radius, and olecranon.

incision.text: Begin 3-5 cm above the joint on the lateral ridge and extend posterior to the radial head onto proximal forearm; place it slightly more posterior than the adult incision.

superficial_interval.text: Open fascia on the lateral ridge and develop the interval between brachioradialis and triceps, continuing anterior to anconeus.

deep_interval.text: Open capsule anteriorly over capitellum toward radial head; elevate only the anterior tissue needed for visualization and preserve posterior fragment attachments.

layers.text: Skin, lateral fascia, brachioradialis-triceps interval, extensor/anconeus border, capsule, then capitellum and lateral condyle.

structures_encountered.text: Brachioradialis, triceps, extensor origin, anconeus, capsule, capitellum, radial head, and lateral-condyle fragment are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Radial nerve and its branches near radial head, posterior fragment vascularity, articular cartilage, physis, and lateral collateral ligament are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Do not strip the posterolateral fragment attachments and do not place a lever retractor anteriorly near the radial nerve.

retraction_hazards.text: Use smooth soft-tissue retraction; anterior levering risks radial nerve injury and posterior stripping risks fragment devascularization.

exposure.text: Exposes lateral condyle, capitellum, radiocapitellar joint, and anterior articular surface for direct reduction.

limitations.text: The approach does not expose the medial column and aggressive posterior extension threatens fragment blood supply.

extensions.text: Release anterior capsule or limited anterior brachioradialis/ECRL and posterior triceps attachments only as required for visualization.

indications.text: Use for displaced lateral-condyle or capitellar fractures, unstable lateral-ligament avulsion, and selected irreducible supracondylar fractures.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid unnecessary open exposure when closed reduction provides congruent stable alignment and avoid this isolated corridor for medial or bicondylar pathology.

implant_implications.text: Select wire or screw trajectories that stabilize the fragment without violating the joint, physis, or preserved posterior vascular attachments.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm articular congruity and fixation on AP, lateral, internal-oblique views and use arthrography when the cartilaginous surface is not directly visible.

closure.text: Repair capsule, muscle-fascial interval, and skin with absorbable sutures without strangulating preserved posterior tissues.

complications.text: Complications include nonunion, malunion, lateral overgrowth, fishtail deformity, growth arrest, stiffness, infection, radial neuropathy, and osteonecrosis.

bailouts.text: If the joint surface cannot be judged, use arthrogram and limited capsular extension rather than circumferential fragment stripping.

questions.question: Which attachments protect fragment blood supply?
questions.answer: The posterior and posterolateral soft-tissue attachments.

questions.question: Which nerve is endangered near radial head?
questions.answer: The radial nerve as it divides into superficial and deep branches.

questions.question: Which view best profiles lateral-condyle displacement?

approaches.name: Pediatric medial approach to the distal humerus
approaches.corridor: Medial supracondylar exposure with direct identification and protection of the ulnar nerve

sources.title: The necessity of ulnar nerve exploration and translocation in open reduction of medial humeral epicondyle fractures in children
Operative versus non-operative management of pediatric medial epicondyle fractures: a systematic review

procedure_applications.condition: A medial epicondyle fracture requires open reduction or direct ulnar-nerve assessment
A mini-open exposure is chosen for safe medial crossed-pin placement

positioning.text: Position supine with arm supported, medial elbow accessible, and fluoroscopy able to obtain orthogonal views without stressing fixation.

setup.text: Document ulnar-nerve function, plan fragment and flexor-pronator management, and decide whether only a mini-open pin window or full exposure is required.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark medial supracondylar ridge, medial epicondyle, olecranon, ulnar groove, and flexor-pronator mass.

incision.text: Center a 2-3 cm extensile incision across medial epicondyle; for pin visualization alone, use a roughly 1.5 cm incision with blunt subcutaneous dissection.

superficial_interval.text: Identify and protect the posterior branch of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, then locate the ulnar nerve proximally, in its groove, and between FCU heads.

deep_interval.text: Retract the protected ulnar nerve gently, release medial intermuscular septum proximally as needed, and retract flexor-pronator mass anteriorly for capsular access.

layers.text: Skin, cutaneous-nerve plane, ulnar-nerve plane, medial septum/flexor-pronator origin, capsule, then medial distal humerus.

structures_encountered.text: Medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, ulnar nerve, FCU heads, medial septum, flexor-pronator origin, capsule, and medial epicondyle are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Ulnar nerve and its FCU motor branch, medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, physis, and medial collateral ligament are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Preserve the first FCU motor branch if transposition is necessary and never place a medial pin without knowing the ulnar-nerve position.

retraction_hazards.text: Use a broad smooth retractor or soft loop without sustained ulnar-nerve traction; avoid focal pressure behind medial epicondyle.

exposure.text: Exposes medial epicondyle for reduction and fixation, permits ulnar-nerve exploration, and provides direct protection during medial pin insertion.

limitations.text: Opening the joint medially is not an ideal primary exposure for routine pediatric supracondylar fracture reduction.

extensions.text: Release medial septum approximately 3 cm proximally or open capsule longitudinally only when the pathology requires broader medial access.

indications.text: Use for medial epicondyle fixation, ulnar-nerve exploration, and mini-open protection during crossed K-wire fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid routine extensile medial arthrotomy for a reducible supracondylar fracture without medial pathology or nerve concern.

implant_implications.text: Place screws or wires under direct ulnar-nerve protection and verify that implants do not tether nerve, violate joint, or injure the physis.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use AP, lateral, and oblique images to confirm reduction and that medial pins or screws remain extra-articular with safe trajectories.

closure.text: Repair capsule when opened, restore flexor-pronator tissues, confirm a tension-free ulnar nerve, and close with fine absorbable sutures.

complications.text: Complications include ulnar neuropathy, sensory neuroma, stiffness, nonunion, valgus instability, growth disturbance, infection, and symptomatic hardware.

bailouts.text: If reduction is blocked by incarcerated fragment or nerve, enlarge under direct visualization rather than force percutaneous fixation.

questions.question: Which cutaneous nerve commonly crosses the incision?
questions.answer: The posterior branch of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve.

questions.question: What does a mini-open medial incision accomplish?
questions.answer: Direct visualization and protection of the ulnar nerve during medial pin placement.

questions.question: Which motor branch must be preserved?

approaches.name: Pediatric posterior distal-humerus approach without olecranon osteotomy
approaches.region: posterior pediatric elbow and distal humerus
approaches.corridor: Posterior medial, lateral, combined triceps-flip, or midline triceps window without olecranon osteotomy

sources.title: Evidence-based treatment strategies and systematic review of pediatric AO/OTA type C2 distal-humerus fractures
Surgical approaches for ORIF of intra-articular distal humerus fractures in adults

procedure_applications.condition: A pediatric T- or Y-type distal-humerus fracture requires posterior articular and column exposure

positioning.text: Position lateral decubitus with arm supported and elbow capable of hyperflexion to move olecranon out of the articular view.

setup.text: Select medial, lateral, combined, or midline window according to fracture geometry and plan ulnar- and radial-nerve thresholds before extending exposure.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark posterior humeral shaft, medial/lateral epicondyles, olecranon, ulnar crest, and ulnar-nerve course.

incision.text: Begin about one child-hand breadth above olecranon, curve laterally around its tip, and continue 2-4 cm along ulnar crest to create an ulnar-based flap.

superficial_interval.text: Raise an ulnar-based flap and identify the selected medial, lateral, or exact midline triceps window.

deep_interval.text: For medial/lateral windows mobilize triceps from the corresponding humeral side; for midline split tendon to olecranon and extend 3-4 cm above fracture, preserving extensor continuity.

layers.text: Skin, ulnar-based flap, triceps fascia/window, limited olecranon cartilage-periosteal sleeve, capsule, then posterior distal humerus.

structures_encountered.text: Ulnar nerve, triceps, anconeus, medial/lateral septa, olecranon fossa, posterior capsule, and distal-humeral joint are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Ulnar nerve medially, radial nerve with proximal lateral extension, triceps insertion, olecranon cartilage/periosteum, physis, and posterior periosteal hinge are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Preserve sufficient triceps tendon, insertion, and ulnar periosteum for extensor continuity; identify radial nerve before proximal lateral extension.

retraction_hazards.text: Use smooth broad retractors and avoid ulnar-nerve traction, forceful proximal triceps retraction, or excessive stripping of posterior periosteum.

exposure.text: Combined medial and lateral windows or a midline split expose posterior columns, olecranon fossa, and joint without creating an olecranon osteotomy.

limitations.text: Posterior exposure compromises the stabilizing posterior periosteum in extension-type supracondylar fractures and is not routine for those injuries.

extensions.text: Combine medial and lateral windows for a triceps flip or extend a midline split proximally only with radial-nerve awareness.

indications.text: Use for pediatric T- or Y-type intercondylar distal-humerus fractures requiring posterior articular access.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid as the routine exposure for extension-type supracondylar fractures because posterior periosteal disruption removes a stabilizing structure.

implant_implications.text: Plan fixation through chosen windows while maintaining enough olecranon-triceps-periosteal tissue for repair and keeping implants away from ulnar nerve.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use AP, lateral, and oblique views through unrestricted elbow motion to verify articular reduction, column alignment, and implant containment.

closure.text: Repair capsule, reattach any cartilage-periosteal olecranon sleeve, close triceps and fascia anatomically, and confirm tension-free nerve positions.

complications.text: Complications include ulnar or radial neuropathy, triceps weakness, stiffness, growth disturbance, nonunion, infection, heterotopic ossification, and fixation failure.

bailouts.text: Combine the medial and lateral windows when one is inadequate, preserving extensor continuity rather than creating an unplanned osteotomy.

questions.question: How does elbow flexion affect visualization?
questions.answer: At about 110 degrees the olecranon clears the posterior joint surface most completely.

questions.question: Which nerve limits proximal lateral extension?
Why avoid this approach for routine extension supracondylar fractures?
questions.answer: It compromises the stabilizing posterior periosteum.
